% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
As LLM outputs re-enter training corpora and seed further generation, understanding how recursive generation reshapes text distributions is critical for data provenance and corpus curation---yet existing detectors answer only the binary human-or-machine question, ignoring \emph{generation depth}: we introduce \emph{depth profiling} to address this gap.
We decompose distributional drift under recursive generation into location and shape components, revealing an asymmetry we term \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): across eight base-model generators from five families, NLL location features drift monotonically with depth (effect size $d{=}0.74$--$1.05$) while three shape features remain near-stationary ($d < 0.10$), with entropy std intermediate ($d{=}0.46$)---a ${\geq}8{\times}$ effect-size gap.
Prior work documents \emph{what converges}; the central finding here is \emph{what is approximately preserved}: shape stability complements location drift for ordinal depth grading without per-generator calibration, achieving leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), cross-model binary F1\,=\,0.830, and 3-class F1\,=\,0.762 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation (gen-0 seeds shared across generators; \S\ref{sec:generation}); an end-to-end classifier reaches 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (6-gen LOGO; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}).
Instruction tuning compresses DDR, bounding current applicability to base models.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	An estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications already contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}. As these outputs re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} and seed further generation, text accumulates at varying \emph{generation depths}; each successive cycle reshapes distributional properties in ways that matter for data provenance, corpus auditing, and contamination monitoring in base-model pretraining corpora \cite{ccnet,dsir} as well as model collapse analysis \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}. Understanding \emph{how} recursive generation alters text distributions---and which properties change versus which are preserved---is therefore a prerequisite for principled corpus curation, yet current methods address only binary human-or-machine detection \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score}.
5	Base models provide the cleanest substrate to isolate depth effects from alignment-induced changes.
6	We find that recursive generation produces a decomposable depth profile: distributional \emph{location} drifts with depth while \emph{shape} remains stable across generators, an asymmetry sufficient for cross-generator depth prediction.
7	
8	Distributional compression under recursive generation is well-documented \cite{curious_decline,broken_telephone,markovian_chains}, yet existing analyses characterize \emph{that} and \emph{why} convergence occurs without decomposing what drifts from what is preserved.
9	We introduce \emph{depth profiling} (coarse ordinal classification into gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), and decompose this compression into structurally distinct components: across eight base-model generators spanning five architectural families (0.6B--8B), the NLL distribution's central tendency (mean entropy (reference-model NLL), lexical diversity) drifts monotonically with depth while its shape (entropy extremes, tail structure) remains ${\geq}8{\times}$ more stable (effect size $d{=}0.74$--$1.05$ vs.\ $d < 0.10$ for three near-stationary features; entropy std is intermediate ($d{=}0.46$); boundary features show additional nuance; convergent effect-size measures confirm this partition).
10	We term this location/shape asymmetry the \emph{differential depth response} (DDR; Figure~\ref{fig:ddr-trajectory}), an empirical regularity of base-model autoregressive generation that is mechanistically distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion}, which erodes tail coverage via weight updates; DDR instead analyzes fixed-parameter inference chains.
11	The stationary shape component complements location drift for depth prediction without per-generator calibration.
12	
13	\begin{figure*}[t!]
14	\centering
15	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_ddr_trajectory.pdf}
16	\caption{Feature trajectories across generation depth ($y$-axis: $z$-scored feature values). \textbf{Top row (drifting)}: entropy mean and hapax ratio decline monotonically across all eight generators ($|\rho| > 0.59$). \textbf{Bottom row (stationary)}: entropy max and tail decay remain flat ($|\rho| < 0.07$). Colored lines: individual generators; diamonds: cross-generator mean (blue for drifting, amber for stationary). This dichotomy defines the DDR.}
17	\label{fig:ddr-trajectory}
18	\end{figure*}
19	We focus on base (pretrained) models; instruction tuning degrades depth signal (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).
20	
21	As a proof of concept, a lightweight 7-feature ensemble informed by DDR achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, matching multi-detector ensembles at ${\sim}2.4\times$ lower cost; an end-to-end QLoRA classifier reaches 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (6-gen LOGO; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming that the depth signal extends well beyond handcrafted features.
22	
23	Our contributions:
24	\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
25	    \item \textbf{Empirical decomposition (DDR).} Across eight generators from five families, we decompose inference-chain drift into two primary response zones---drifting ($d{=}0.74$--$1.05$) vs.\ near-stationary ($d < 0.10$)---plus one intermediate feature ($d{=}0.46$). Where prior work documents \emph{what converges} \cite{curious_decline,markovian_chains}, DDR identifies \emph{what is approximately preserved}, an empirical regularity with analytical utility for depth classification without per-generator calibration. DDR is a descriptive empirical finding; the classification value lies in this decomposition rather than the classifier itself.
26	    \item \textbf{Task formulation and evaluation suite.} We define generation depth classification as an ordinal prediction task and construct a controlled dataset of 37K texts from eight generators across five families (0.6B--8B; exploratory evidence extends to 14B, Appendix~\ref{app:9gen-scale}), with leave-one-generator-out cross-validation as the primary evaluation protocol.
27	    \item \textbf{Scope characterization.} Systematic evaluation across temperature, prompt type, instruction tuning, model scale, domain transfer, and perturbation robustness maps the operational envelope of depth profiling.
28	\end{enumerate}
29

2	
3	To assess the DDR partition structure and determine whether the drifting/non-drifting split is data-driven, we apply $k$-means clustering ($k \in \{2,3,4,5\}$) to the seven features in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space (Table~\ref{tab:clustering}).
4	
5	\begin{table}[ht]
6	\centering
7	\small
8	\caption{$k$-means clustering of 7 features in $(|\rho|, d)$ space.}
9	\label{tab:clustering}
10	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
11	\begin{tabular}{ccp{5.5cm}}
12	\toprule
13	$k$ & Silhouette & Clusters \\
14	\midrule
15	2 & \textbf{0.660} & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} \\
16	3 & 0.532 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
17	4 & 0.527 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
18	\bottomrule
19	\end{tabular}}
20	\end{table}
21	
22	The primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.660) is the strongest cluster structure.
23	At $k{=}3$, entropy min forms its own cluster rather than joining the near-stationary group because its pooled $|\rho|{=}0.40$ (driven by the gen-0/gen-1 boundary) places it far from other near-stationary features in $\rho$ space.
24	The 3/1/3 DDR partition resolves this by using the gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ Cohen's $d$ ($d{=}0.03$) to place entropy min in the near-stationary group, a domain-informed refinement that unsupervised clustering cannot recover from pooled statistics alone.
25	At $k{=}4$ (silhouette\,=\,0.571), entropy std separates from the near-stationary group, consistent with its intermediate DDR classification.
26	
27	\paragraph{Exhaustive partition enumeration.}
28	To confirm that the three-vs-four split is optimal rather than incidental, we enumerate all $\binom{7}{3}{=}35$ possible ways to assign three features to a ``drifting'' group and the remaining four to ``non-drifting,'' computing the silhouette score for each partition in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
29	The observed DDR partition (\{entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio\}) achieves the highest silhouette (0.660), with a gap of 0.18 to the second-ranked split; 20 of 35 partitions produce negative silhouette scores.
30	
31	\paragraph{Per-generator replication.}
32	To rule out the possibility that the pooled silhouette is an artifact of mixing heterogeneous generators, we repeat the $(|\rho|, d)$ clustering independently for each of the eight generators.
33	Every generator recovers the identical \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} vs.\ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} partition, with silhouette scores ranging from 0.505 (Pythia-1B) to 0.760 (Mistral-7B-v0.3; mean\,=\,0.651).
34	No generator falls below the 0.50 moderate-structure threshold, confirming that the two-cluster structure is a per-generator property rather than a pooling artifact.
35	
36	\subsection*{TOST Equivalence Bound Sensitivity}
37	\label{app:tost-sensitivity}
38	
39	Table~\ref{tab:tost-sensitivity} shows the fraction of generators for which each feature passes the TOST equivalence test (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $\alpha{=}0.05$) at three equivalence bounds $\varepsilon$.
40	
41	\begin{table}[ht]
42	\centering
43	\small
44	\caption{TOST equivalence pass rate across 8 generators at varying $\varepsilon$.}
45	\label{tab:tost-sensitivity}
46	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
47	\begin{tabular}{llccc}
48	\toprule
49	\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.15}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.20}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.25}$ \\
50	\midrule
51	\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
52	 & TTR & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
53	 & hapax ratio & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
54	\midrule
55	Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
56	\midrule
57	\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 7/8 & 8/8 & 8/8 \\
58	 & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 6/8 & 6/8 & 6/8 \\
59	 & tail decay & 4/8 & 4/8 & 7/8 \\
60	\bottomrule
61	\end{tabular}}
62	\end{table}
63	
64	The partition is robust to the equivalence bound: drifting features reject equivalence at all $\varepsilon$ for all generators, while entropy min passes even at the stricter bound $\varepsilon{=}0.15$ (7/8 generators).
65	Tail decay is the most $\varepsilon$-sensitive near-stationary feature, passing 4/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ but 7/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.25$; the four non-passing generators show $|d|{=}0.15$--$0.22$, still well below the drifting threshold ($d > 0.50$).
66	Entropy max is stable across all three bounds (6/8), with the two failures (Pythia-1B $d{=}0.21$, Pythia-2.8B $d{=}0.25$) reflecting same-family reference affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model.
67	
68	\paragraph{TOST margin rationale.}
69	We adopt $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ as the primary equivalence bound, corresponding to Cohen's ``small effect'' threshold ($d{=}0.20$; \citealp{cohen1988statistical}).
70	This choice reflects a principled smallest effect size of interest (SESOI): effects below $d{=}0.20$ are conventionally negligible and unlikely to carry practical discriminative value for depth classification.
71	The bound is conservative relative to the drifting--stationary gap ($d_{\min}^{\text{drift}}{=}0.74$ vs.\ $\varepsilon{=}0.20$, a $3.7{\times}$ margin), ensuring that the equivalence test has adequate power to confirm near-stationarity without risk of misclassifying genuinely drifting features.
72	As Table~\ref{tab:tost-sensitivity} shows, conclusions are qualitatively identical at $\varepsilon{=}0.15$ and $\varepsilon{=}0.25$, confirming insensitivity to the specific bound choice.
73	LOFO analysis independently corroborates this boundary: near-stationary features contribute ${<}2$\,pp marginal importance (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}), empirically validating $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ as a task-relevant threshold.
74	
75	\paragraph{Threshold sensitivity.}
76	To address concerns about the sensitivity of the drifting-boundary threshold,
77	we sweep $|d|$ from $0.10$ to $0.80$ in increments of $0.05$ and record the
78	resulting binary partition (drifting vs.\ stationary) along with the silhouette
79	score in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
80	Across the entire range, only \emph{three} distinct partitions emerge,
81	reflecting natural gaps between feature clusters rather than threshold artifacts.
82	The three-feature drifting set (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio)
83	is stable across $|d| \in [0.50,\, 0.75]$ with a silhouette of $0.660$---the
84	peak value in the sweep.
85	Including the intermediate feature entropy std ($d{=}0.46$) yields a
86	4/3 partition stable across $|d| \in [0.10,\, 0.45]$ (silhouette\,=\,0.451).
87	The partition used in our analysis corresponds to the peak-silhouette region,
88	confirming that the drifting/stationary boundary reflects a natural gap in the
89	$(|\rho|, d)$ landscape rather than an artifact of a particular
90	threshold choice.
91	
92	\paragraph{Partition stability across $\varepsilon$ thresholds.}
93	\label{app:epsilon-sweep}
94	
95	The DDR partition classifies features as non-stationary ($d \geq \varepsilon$) or stationary ($d < \varepsilon$) based on pooled Cohen's $d$ (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
96	Table~\ref{tab:epsilon-sweep} reports the critical $\varepsilon$ at which each feature's classification changes; the three drifting and three near-stationary features maintain their classification for all $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$.
97	
98	\begin{table}[ht]
99	\centering
100	\small
101	\caption{Partition stability under varying $\varepsilon$. Critical threshold: the $\varepsilon$ above which a feature is reclassified as stationary. The drifting/near-stationary split is invariant for $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$; only entropy std ($d{=}0.46$) changes at $\varepsilon > 0.46$.}
102	\label{tab:epsilon-sweep}
103	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
104	\begin{tabular}{llcc}
105	\toprule
106	\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Pooled $d$} & \textbf{Stationary at $\varepsilon >$} \\
107	\midrule
108	\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 1.05 & 1.05 \\
109	 & TTR & 0.81 & 0.81 \\
110	 & hapax ratio & 0.74 & 0.74 \\
111	\midrule
112	Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.46 & 0.46 \\
113	\midrule
114	\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.06 & 0.06 \\
115	 & tail decay & 0.09 & 0.09 \\
116	 & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.016 & 0.016 \\
117	\bottomrule
118	\end{tabular}}
119	\end{table}
120	
121	\noindent The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$: the three drifting features remain non-stationary at all $\varepsilon < 0.74$, the three near-stationary features remain stationary at all $\varepsilon > 0.09$, and only entropy std changes classification (becoming stationary at $\varepsilon > 0.46$), confirming it as the sole threshold-sensitive feature.
122	The minimum gap between adjacent zone boundaries ($d_{\text{hapax}} - d_{\sigma_H} = 0.28$) exceeds typical effect-size estimation uncertainty, providing a margin against sampling noise.
123	
124	\subsection*{Holdout Generator Split Validation}
125	\label{app:holdout-split}
126	
127	To confirm the DDR partition is not an artifact of the specific generator pool, we split the eight generators into disjoint selection (4) and validation (4) sets, compute per-subset pooled $(|\rho|, d)$, and check whether all seven features receive the same zone assignment in both subsets.

\subsection*{Data-Driven Clustering}

To assess the DDR partition structure and determine whether the drifting/non-drifting split is data-driven, we apply $k$-means clustering ($k \in \{2,3,4,5\}$) to the seven features in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space (Table~\ref{tab:clustering}).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{$k$-means clustering of 7 features in $(|\rho|, d)$ space.}
\label{tab:clustering}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{ccp{5.5cm}}
\toprule
$k$ & Silhouette & Clusters \\
\midrule
2 & \textbf{0.660} & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} \\
3 & 0.532 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
4 & 0.527 & \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\max}$, tail\} $\mid$ \{$\sigma_H$\} $\mid$ \{$H_{\min}$\} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.660) is the strongest cluster structure.
At $k{=}3$, entropy min forms its own cluster rather than joining the near-stationary group because its pooled $|\rho|{=}0.40$ (driven by the gen-0/gen-1 boundary) places it far from other near-stationary features in $\rho$ space.
The 3/1/3 DDR partition resolves this by using the gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ Cohen's $d$ ($d{=}0.03$) to place entropy min in the near-stationary group, a domain-informed refinement that unsupervised clustering cannot recover from pooled statistics alone.
At $k{=}4$ (silhouette\,=\,0.571), entropy std separates from the near-stationary group, consistent with its intermediate DDR classification.

\paragraph{Exhaustive partition enumeration.}
To confirm that the three-vs-four split is optimal rather than incidental, we enumerate all $\binom{7}{3}{=}35$ possible ways to assign three features to a ``drifting'' group and the remaining four to ``non-drifting,'' computing the silhouette score for each partition in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
The observed DDR partition (\{entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio\}) achieves the highest silhouette (0.660), with a gap of 0.18 to the second-ranked split; 20 of 35 partitions produce negative silhouette scores.

\paragraph{Per-generator replication.}
To rule out the possibility that the pooled silhouette is an artifact of mixing heterogeneous generators, we repeat the $(|\rho|, d)$ clustering independently for each of the eight generators.
Every generator recovers the identical \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} vs.\ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} partition, with silhouette scores ranging from 0.505 (Pythia-1B) to 0.760 (Mistral-7B-v0.3; mean\,=\,0.651).
No generator falls below the 0.50 moderate-structure threshold, confirming that the two-cluster structure is a per-generator property rather than a pooling artifact.

\subsection*{TOST Equivalence Bound Sensitivity}
\label{app:tost-sensitivity}

Table~\ref{tab:tost-sensitivity} shows the fraction of generators for which each feature passes the TOST equivalence test (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $\alpha{=}0.05$) at three equivalence bounds $\varepsilon$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{TOST equivalence pass rate across 8 generators at varying $\varepsilon$.}
\label{tab:tost-sensitivity}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.15}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.20}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.25}$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
 & TTR & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 7/8 & 8/8 & 8/8 \\
 & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 6/8 & 6/8 & 6/8 \\
 & tail decay & 4/8 & 4/8 & 7/8 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The partition is robust to the equivalence bound: drifting features reject equivalence at all $\varepsilon$ for all generators, while entropy min passes even at the stricter bound $\varepsilon{=}0.15$ (7/8 generators).
Tail decay is the most $\varepsilon$-sensitive near-stationary feature, passing 4/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ but 7/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.25$; the four non-passing generators show $|d|{=}0.15$--$0.22$, still well below the drifting threshold ($d > 0.50$).
Entropy max is stable across all three bounds (6/8), with the two failures (Pythia-1B $d{=}0.21$, Pythia-2.8B $d{=}0.25$) reflecting same-family reference affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model.

\paragraph{TOST margin rationale.}
We adopt $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ as the primary equivalence bound, corresponding to Cohen's ``small effect'' threshold ($d{=}0.20$; \citealp{cohen1988statistical}).
This choice reflects a principled smallest effect size of interest (SESOI): effects below $d{=}0.20$ are conventionally negligible and unlikely to carry practical discriminative value for depth classification.
The bound is conservative relative to the drifting--stationary gap ($d_{\min}^{\text{drift}}{=}0.74$ vs.\ $\varepsilon{=}0.20$, a $3.7{\times}$ margin), ensuring that the equivalence test has adequate power to confirm near-stationarity without risk of misclassifying genuinely drifting features.
As Table~\ref{tab:tost-sensitivity} shows, conclusions are qualitatively identical at $\varepsilon{=}0.15$ and $\varepsilon{=}0.25$, confirming insensitivity to the specific bound choice.
LOFO analysis independently corroborates this boundary: near-stationary features contribute ${<}2$\,pp marginal importance (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}), empirically validating $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ as a task-relevant threshold.

\paragraph{Threshold sensitivity.}
To address concerns about the sensitivity of the drifting-boundary threshold,
we sweep $|d|$ from $0.10$ to $0.80$ in increments of $0.05$ and record the
resulting binary partition (drifting vs.\ stationary) along with the silhouette
score in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
Across the entire range, only \emph{three} distinct partitions emerge,
reflecting natural gaps between feature clusters rather than threshold artifacts.
The three-feature drifting set (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio)
is stable across $|d| \in [0.50,\, 0.75]$ with a silhouette of $0.660$---the
peak value in the sweep.
Including the intermediate feature entropy std ($d{=}0.46$) yields a
4/3 partition stable across $|d| \in [0.10,\, 0.45]$ (silhouette\,=\,0.451).
The partition used in our analysis corresponds to the peak-silhouette region,
confirming that the drifting/stationary boundary reflects a natural gap in the
$(|\rho|, d)$ landscape rather than an artifact of a particular
threshold choice.

\paragraph{Partition stability across $\varepsilon$ thresholds.}
\label{app:epsilon-sweep}

The DDR partition classifies features as non-stationary ($d \geq \varepsilon$) or stationary ($d < \varepsilon$) based on pooled Cohen's $d$ (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Table~\ref{tab:epsilon-sweep} reports the critical $\varepsilon$ at which each feature's classification changes; the three drifting and three near-stationary features maintain their classification for all $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Partition stability under varying $\varepsilon$. Critical threshold: the $\varepsilon$ above which a feature is reclassified as stationary. The drifting/near-stationary split is invariant for $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$; only entropy std ($d{=}0.46$) changes at $\varepsilon > 0.46$.}
\label{tab:epsilon-sweep}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Pooled $d$} & \textbf{Stationary at $\varepsilon >$} \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 1.05 & 1.05 \\
 & TTR & 0.81 & 0.81 \\
 & hapax ratio & 0.74 & 0.74 \\
\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.46 & 0.46 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Near-stat.} & $H_{\max}$ (ent.\ max) & 0.06 & 0.06 \\
 & tail decay & 0.09 & 0.09 \\
 & $H_{\min}$ (ent.\ min) & 0.016 & 0.016 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\noindent The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$: the three drifting features remain non-stationary at all $\varepsilon < 0.74$, the three near-stationary features remain stationary at all $\varepsilon > 0.09$, and only entropy std changes classification (becoming stationary at $\varepsilon > 0.46$), confirming it as the sole threshold-sensitive feature.
The minimum gap between adjacent zone boundaries ($d_{\text{hapax}} - d_{\sigma_H} = 0.28$) exceeds typical effect-size estimation uncertainty, providing a margin against sampling noise.

\subsection*{Holdout Generator Split Validation}
\label{app:holdout-split}

To confirm the DDR partition is not an artifact of the specific generator pool, we split the eight generators into disjoint selection (4) and validation (4) sets, compute per-subset pooled $(|\rho|, d)$, and check whether all seven features receive the same zone assignment in both subsets.
We evaluate two complementary splits to avoid dependence on a single partition:
Split~A selects \{Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B, Llama);
Split~B selects \{Pythia-1B, Qwen3-0.6B, OLMo, Mistral\} (validation: Pythia-2.8B, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, Llama).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Holdout split validation of the DDR partition. Selection (sel) and validation (val) $|\rho|$ and $d$ for two disjoint 4/4 generator splits. Zone assignment is identical across all four subsets for every feature.}
\label{tab:holdout-split}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcccccc}
\toprule
& & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split A}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Split B}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){3-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-8}
\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ & sel $|\rho|$ & val $|\rho|$ & $\Delta|\rho|$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 & 0.60 & 0.58 & 0.02 \\

\midrule
Intermediate & $\sigma_H$ (ent.\ std) & 0.19 & 0.21 & 0.02 & 0.22 & 0.17 & 0.05 \\
\midrule

 & tail decay & 0.10 & 0.08 & 0.02 & 0.11 & 0.07 & 0.04 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Under simple joint $(|\rho|, d)$ thresholds, both splits produce a 3/2/2 partition: entropy min is classified as a second intermediate feature due to its elevated pooled $|\rho|$ (0.36--0.39).
However, entropy min's binary (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) $d$ values are uniformly below 0.06 across all four split${\times}$subset combinations, consistent with near-stationarity on the task-relevant metric; its pooled $|\rho|$ reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary rather than sustained drift.
Five of seven features are unambiguously classified under any reasonable criterion; entropy min's boundary status is resolved by the binary-task $d$ criterion.

\caption{Holdout split validation in $(|\rho|, d)$ space. Filled markers: selection set; hollow: validation set. Zone assignments are identical across subsets; selection/validation pairs cluster tightly for all features.}
\label{fig:holdout-scatter}
\end{figure}

\centering
\small
\caption{Effect size comparison (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $N$\,=\,29{,}095). Glass's $\Delta$ uses the gen-1 SD as denominator; Cliff's $\delta$ thresholds follow Romano et al.\ (2006): $|\delta| < 0.147$ negligible, $< 0.33$ small, $< 0.474$ medium, otherwise large.}
\label{tab:effect-sizes}
\begin{tabular}{llrrr}

\textbf{Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & \textbf{$|d|$} & \textbf{$|\Delta|$} & \textbf{$|\delta|$} \\

1	\subsection*{Instruction-Tuned Model Results}
2	
3	Table~\ref{tab:instruct} summarizes depth classification under instruction tuning for three model families.
4	All results use within-model 5-fold CV on single-generator chains; LOGO evaluation is available for two models but uses earlier generator subsets (5--6 generators), so cross-model numbers are not directly comparable across rows.
5	
6	\begin{table}[ht]
7	\centering
8	\small
9	\caption{Depth classification: base vs.\ instruction-tuned models (within-model 5-fold CV). $\rho$: Spearman correlation of entropy mean with depth. Rev.: number of features (out of 7) whose $\rho$ reverses sign under instruction tuning.}
10	\label{tab:instruct}
11	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
12	\begin{tabular}{lcc cc cc c}
13	\toprule
14	& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{3-class F1}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{Binary F1}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{$\boldsymbol{\rho}$\textbf{(ent.\ mean)}} & \\
15	\cmidrule(lr){2-3} \cmidrule(lr){4-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-7}
16	\textbf{Model} & Base & Instruct & Base & Instruct & Base & Instruct & \textbf{Rev.} \\
17	\midrule
18	OLMo-2-1B       & 0.754 & 0.575 & 0.845 & 0.813 & $-$0.64 & $+$0.48 & 6/7 \\
19	Qwen3-1.7B      & 0.769 & 0.732 & 0.861 & 0.875 & $-$0.60 & $+$0.48 & 6/7 \\
20	Llama-3.2-3B    & 0.742 & 0.544 & 0.849 & 0.838 & $-$0.63 & $+$0.23 & 3/7 \\
21	\bottomrule
22	\end{tabular}}
23	\end{table}
24	
25	Instruction tuning degrades 3-class F1 by 3.7--19.9\,pp across all three families, while binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) changes remain small ($|\Delta| \leq 3.2$\,pp).
26	The asymmetry indicates that instruction tuning primarily disrupts the gen-0/gen-1 boundary (human vs.\ first-generation), consistent with RLHF shifting the output distribution away from human-like text.
27	Entropy-mean $\rho$ reverses sign for all three models ($-0.60$--$-0.64$ base $\rightarrow$ $+0.23$--$+0.48$ instruct), and 6 of 7 features reverse for OLMo and Qwen vs.\ 3 of 7 for Llama.
28	This pattern is consistent with instruction tuning shifting the generation attractor rather than eliminating iterative dynamics (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
29	
30	\paragraph{Retraining on instruction-tuned data.}
31	To test whether the depth signal persists under instruction tuning with reversed polarity, we retrain the XGBoost classifier on instruction-tuned feature data (Table~\ref{tab:instruct-retrain}).
32	
33	\begin{table}[ht]
34	\centering
35	\small
36	\caption{Classification recovery under instruction-tuned retraining (binary-only: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, gen-0 excluded from training and evaluation). Base$\rightarrow$Inst: base-trained classifier tested on instruct data. Note: Table~\ref{tab:instruct} reports higher instruct binary F1 (e.g., OLMo 0.813) because it uses 3-class training with binary evaluation, where gen-0 in training helps the classifier learn the feature space.}
37	\label{tab:instruct-retrain}
38	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
39	\toprule
40	\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Base$\rightarrow$Inst} & \textbf{Retrained} & \textbf{$\Delta$} \\
41	\midrule
42	OLMo-2-1B-Inst   & 0.321 & 0.590 & $+$0.269 \\
43	Qwen3-1.7B-Inst  & 0.500 & 0.660 & $+$0.160 \\
44	Qwen3-0.6B-Inst  & 0.532 & 0.600 & $+$0.068 \\
45	\bottomrule
46	\end{tabular}
47	\end{table}
48	
49	Retraining recovers substantial within-model performance ($+$6.8--26.9\,pp), but the retrained F1 (0.590--0.660) remains below base-model levels (0.69--0.72).
50	Three-generator instruct LOGO yields binary F1\,=\,0.487, indicating weak cross-generator transfer under instruction tuning.
51	
52	\paragraph{DDR structure under instruction tuning.}
53	$k{=}2$ clustering in $(|\rho|, d)$ space on pooled instruct features yields silhouette\,=\,0.372 (vs.\ 0.660 for base models), indicating that the clean drifting/non-drifting partition is substantially compressed.

The binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) is unaffected because both classes are generated under identical domain and decoding conditions; recursive drift is a relative change that does not depend on absolute calibration.
This pattern provides additional evidence that DDR captures base-model generation dynamics rather than domain-specific text properties: depth signal remains robust even when the human-vs-machine boundary becomes less distinct.

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, which confirms the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

\paragraph{Equivalence testing.}
We apply a two one-sided $t$-test (TOST) with a $\pm$2\% relative margin (equivalence bounds $\pm$0.047 on the ppl scale) to formally assess whether the depth-aware and random subsampling conditions produce practically indistinguishable perplexity.
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951): size-matched (random) ppl\,=\,2.367 vs.\ depth 0--1 ppl\,=\,2.387, $\Delta$\,=\,0.020.
TOST confirms equivalence ($p = 1.1 \times 10^{-4}$); the two curation strategies yield practically indistinguishable downstream quality within the $\pm$2\% margin.
Cross-seed standard deviation is below 0.001 for both variants.

Comparing the full dataset ($n$\,=\,12{,}299, ppl\,=\,2.335) against the depth-filtered subset ($n$\,=\,3{,}951, ppl\,=\,2.387): TOST \emph{rejects} equivalence (minimum equivalence margin\,=\,0.053, exceeding the $\pm$2\% bound), which confirms that data quantity drives perplexity reduction beyond what depth-aware selection can recover.

Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training; at fixed sample count, depth-aware curation is statistically equivalent to uninformed random subsampling.

\subsection*{Margin Sensitivity Analysis}

To assess the robustness of the equivalence conclusion to margin choice, we repeat the TOST procedure across multiple equivalence margins \cite{lakens_equivalence}, following the recommendation to report sensitivity across plausible bounds rather than relying on a single threshold (Table~\ref{tab:tost-margins}).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{TOST equivalence testing across multiple margins. ``Equiv?'' indicates whether equivalence is established at $\alpha = 0.05$.}
\label{tab:tost-margins}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Comparison} & \textbf{Margin} & \textbf{Equiv?} & \textbf{TOST $p$} \\
\midrule
Full (12{,}299) vs.\ Random (3{,}951) & $\pm$1\% & No & 1.0 \\
                                        & $\pm$2\% & Yes & $1 \times 10^{-6}$ \\
                                        & $\pm$3\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
                                        & $\pm$5\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
\midrule
Full (12{,}299) vs.\ Depth 0--1 (3{,}951) & $\pm$1\% & No & 1.0 \\
                                            & $\pm$2\% & No & 1.0 \\
                                            & $\pm$3\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
                                            & $\pm$5\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The full dataset vs.\ random subsample comparison passes equivalence at the $\pm$2\% margin ($p = 10^{-6}$), while the full vs.\ depth 0--1 comparison requires a $\pm$3\% margin.
In absolute terms, perplexity differences are small: $\Delta$\,=\,0.032 (full vs.\ random, 1.4\% of baseline) and $\Delta$\,=\,0.052 (full vs.\ depth 0--1, 2.2\% of baseline).

Cohen's $d$ values are 86.0 (full vs.\ random) and 119.7 (full vs.\ depth 0--1).
These appear large but are unreliable: with only $n$\,=\,3 seeds per condition, the pooled standard deviation is extremely small ($<$0.001), artificially inflating $d$.
The inflated effect sizes reflect low seed-level variance (confirming reproducibility) rather than practically meaningful perplexity differences.
The TOST framework with pre-specified relative margins provides a more appropriate assessment than Cohen's $d$ in this low-seed regime.
However, with only $n{=}3$ seeds per condition, the TOST results have limited generalizability: the test is valid given observed variance but the conclusion generalizes over only three random seeds. We characterize this as a preliminary observation rather than a definitive null result.

% Appendix — Length Confound Analysis
% Data source: 8-generator LOGO corpus (37,058 samples)

Surface diversity features (TTR, hapax ratio) mechanically depend on text length:
shorter texts yield higher type-token ratios by construction.
If generation depth systematically shortens text, observed depth trends could be length artifacts rather than genuine distributional shifts.
We investigate with three complementary analyses.

\paragraph{(a) Length--depth correlation.}
Spearman rank correlation between word count and generation depth is weak across all eight generators ($|\rho| < 0.14$); depth does not systematically shorten or lengthen text in our corpus.

\paragraph{(b) Length--feature correlations.}
While length--depth correlation is weak, individual features show moderate length dependence:
tail\_decay ($|\rho| = 0.38$), hapax\_ratio ($|\rho| = 0.30$), and TTR ($|\rho| = 0.29$).
Reference-model features show weaker length correlations (entropy\_mean $|\rho| = 0.09$, entropy\_std $|\rho| = 0.18$).
This motivates the length-matched evaluation below: if length mediates some depth--feature association, controlling for length will reduce classification performance.

\paragraph{(c) Length-matched classification.}
We subsample the dataset so that word-count distributions are equalized across depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), then retrain the binary XGBoost classifier under pooled LOGO (8-fold).
Length-matched binary F1\,=\,0.724, down from 0.770 on the unmatched set ($\Delta$\,=\,$-$0.046).
The matched subset is smaller than the full corpus; a random-subsample control at equal $N$ (below) isolates the deconfounding effect from the sample-size reduction.
To distinguish this from a sample-size effect, we run a random-subsample control at equal $N$ without length matching: F1\,=\,0.767, which confirms that the 0.046 drop reflects genuine length deconfounding rather than reduced data.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
Length accounts for approximately 6\% of discriminative performance ($\Delta$\,=\,0.046 out of 0.770).
The majority of the depth signal is length-independent: length-matched F1 (0.724) remains far above chance and significantly above all individual detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
Surface features (TTR, hapax\_ratio) partially co-vary with length, but their depth-discriminative contribution persists after length control, consistent with generation-induced vocabulary compression operating independently of text truncation.
